title: Jansenius grants first impulses of the will are not free, because not in man's power
source_text: XXVIII. Nihilominus agnoscit motus quosdam in voluntate oriri qui propterea tamen liberi non sunt: illos, scilicet, improvisos qui plenum rationis judicium praeveniunt, & qui motus primo primi vocari solent. Quanquam enim ex voluntate sine violentia fluant, deest tamen illis quod est in libertate praecipuum ex ejus sententia, quia in hominis potestate non sunt, & fiunt sine plena rationis advertentia, & invita quodammodo ac repugnante voluntate, quia dum in motus illos reflectitur, eis non consentit, & eos omnino nollet sibi inesse. De Gratia Christi Salvatoris lib. 6. cap. 37.
pass_a_gloss: Nevertheless he acknowledges that certain motions arise in the will which nevertheless are not free on that account: those, namely, unforeseen ones which anticipate the full judgment of reason, and which are wont to be called first-first motions. For although they flow from the will without violence, yet there is lacking in them that which in his opinion is chief in liberty, because they are not in man's power, and come about without full advertence of reason, and with the will in some way unwilling and resisting, because while it reflects upon those motions, it does not consent to them, and would altogether not wish them to be in it. On the Grace of Christ the Saviour book 6. chap. 37.
pass_b_english: He does admit that some motions arise in the will that are not free for all that. These are the sudden ones that run ahead of reason's full judgment, usually called 'first-first motions'.

They come from the will without violence, yet they lack what he takes to be the chief thing in freedom. They are not in a man's power, they happen without reason's full attention, and they happen even against the will's wishes and resistance in some way, since when the will reflects on them it does not consent and would rather not have them in it at all. (On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 37.)

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
